title: Senior's toolkit: configuring and checking the model
summary: How experienced teams organise Fluent API configuration, check what EF Core built, and read constraint errors.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: configuring and checking the model
steps.body: In a real codebase the model has dozens of entities. These are the ways teams keep its configuration tidy, see what EF Core actually built, and turn a database constraint error into a proper response.

toolkit.what: Put each entity's Fluent API setup in its own class instead of one huge `OnModelCreating`. Easy to find, easy to review.
flags: registers every configuration class in one line

toolkit.what: Let the database enforce uniqueness. A check in C# alone loses the race when two requests arrive at once.
flags: a unique index: duplicates are rejected by the database
a partial index, for example unique only among non-deleted rows
a stable name you can match in errors

toolkit.what: Store an enum as its name instead of a number, so the data is readable and reordering the enum does not corrupt it.
flags: any custom conversion, for example a value object to a string
keep the text column a sensible size

toolkit.what: Print the model EF Core built: every entity, property, key, index and relationship. In the debugger, `db.Model` has a DebugView with the same text.
flags: also show annotations such as column types
toolkit.when: a convention did something you did not expect

toolkit.what: Show which context, provider, database and connection the tools will use. Run it first when a `dotnet ef` command hits the wrong database.
flags: pick one when the project has several contexts
list every context the tools can find
the project whose configuration is used

toolkit.what: A constraint violation arrives as `DbUpdateException`; the provider's own exception is in `InnerException`. Map it to a 409 Conflict instead of a 500.

steps.prompt: Signing up with an email that already exists returns HTTP 500, and the log shows this. What is the right fix?
code: Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.DbUpdateException: An error occurred while saving the entity changes. See the inner exception for details.
---> Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.SqliteException (0x80004005): SQLite Error 19: 'UNIQUE constraint failed: Users.Email'.
options: Keep the unique index and catch `DbUpdateException` whose inner exception is the unique violation, returning 409 Conflict
Remove the unique index so the insert succeeds
Check `AnyAsync(u => u.Email == email)` first and remove the index
Wrap `SaveChanges` in `try { } catch { }` and ignore it
steps.explain: Always read the inner exception: it names the constraint. The index is right; it stops duplicates even when two sign-ups race. A pre-check is fine for a friendly message, but only the database can make it safe.

steps.prompt: Configure `User` in its own class: a unique email, and the role stored as text.
Match each tool to the question it answers.
pairs: What keys, indexes and relationships did EF Core build?
Which database will the tools connect to?
Which constraint did the database reject?
How do all my configuration classes get registered?

steps.prompt: `enum OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped }` is stored with the default mapping. Someone adds `Paid` between them. What happens to existing rows?
options: Rows stored as `1` used to mean Shipped and now read as Paid; storing the name with `HasConversion<string>()` avoids this
Nothing: EF Core stores enum names by default
EF Core refuses to start until you migrate
The new value is appended automatically at the end
steps.explain: By default an enum is stored as its number. Inserting a member renumbers the ones after it, silently changing old data. Text costs a few bytes and survives reordering.

steps.prompt: Which provider error code means a duplicate key?

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Give every entity its own configuration class, and put every business rule about uniqueness in an index, not only in C#. When the model surprises you, print `db.Model.ToDebugString()` before you start guessing, and when saving fails, read the inner exception first.
